# Brindlewood Tooling Cooperative - Staff Handbook (excerpt, revision 3, effective 2026-01-01)

## 1. Definitions and Framework

### 1.1 Employment Categories

This handbook applies to all staff of Brindlewood Tooling Cooperative (BTC). Employment is categorized into three distinct types.

A full-time employee is any person employed by BTC on a contract for 35 or more hours per week. Full-time employees are entitled to all benefits described in this handbook.

A part-time employee is any person employed by BTC on a contract for fewer than 35 hours per week. Part-time employees receive benefits on a pro-rata basis unless otherwise specified in this excerpt.

A contractor is a self-employed person or a person employed by an external agency who provides services to BTC but is not directly employed by BTC. Contractors receive only those benefits explicitly listed as available to contractors in this handbook.

### 1.2 Tenure and Reference Date

Tenure is calculated in complete calendar months from an employee's start date. A start date is the first calendar day an employee works for BTC. The reference date for all tenure calculations and eligibility determinations in this handbook is 2026-03-01. All dates and tenure periods are evaluated as of this reference date. For example, an employee who started on 2025-03-15 would have 11 complete months of tenure as of 2026-03-01. An employee who started on 2024-03-01 would have exactly 24 complete months of tenure as of 2026-03-01. Tenure is never rounded and fractional months do not count toward tenure bands.

## 2. Remote Work Eligibility

### 2.1 Full-Time Employees

Full-time employees with at least 6 months of tenure may work remotely. The maximum number of remote work days per week is 3 days. Remote work must be arranged with the employee's immediate supervisor at least one week in advance.

### 2.2 Part-Time Employees

Part-time employees may work remotely up to 2 days per week, provided their employment contract permits remote work. No tenure requirement applies to part-time employees for remote work eligibility.

### 2.3 Workshop Department Exception

Exception: Workshop department staff may never work remotely under any circumstances. This applies to all employment categories—full-time, part-time, and contractors—in the Workshop department.

### 2.4 Logistics Department Remote Work

Logistics department staff may work remotely up to 2 days per week only if two conditions are met: they must be full-time or part-time employees (not contractors), AND they must have at least 3 months of tenure AND they must receive approval from their department head. Department heads may grant an exception to the 3-month tenure requirement for Logistics staff, provided the exception is documented in writing.

### 2.5 Office and Sales Departments

Office and Sales department staff who meet the tenure requirement (at least 6 months for full-time) may work remotely up to 4 days per week.

## 3. Annual Leave Entitlement

### 3.1 Full-Time Employee Leave by Tenure

Full-time employees receive annual leave (paid days off) according to their tenure as calculated on 2026-03-01. Employees with fewer than 2 complete years of tenure receive 20 days of leave per year. Employees with 2 to 5 complete years of tenure (inclusive) receive 23 days of leave per year. Employees with more than 5 complete years of tenure receive 26 days of leave per year.

### 3.2 Part-Time Employee Leave

Part-time employees receive 12 days of leave per year, regardless of tenure. This is a fixed entitlement and does not vary with length of service.

### 3.3 Contractor Leave

Contractors receive no annual leave entitlement. Contractors are not entitled to paid time off.

### 3.4 Leave Carry-Over

Unused leave may be carried over to the next calendar year up to a maximum of 5 days. Any leave in excess of 5 days at the end of a year is forfeited and cannot be carried forward or compensated.

### 3.5 Leave Blackout Period

Workshop staff may not take leave during the blackout period from 2026-12-01 to 2026-12-14 (the first two weeks of December), except in cases of emergency leave. Emergency leave in the blackout period must be approved by the Operations Manager in writing and is limited to genuine emergencies such as serious illness or family bereavement. Planned leave during the blackout period is not permitted for Workshop staff. This blackout period applies every December, following the same calendar dates each year. Workshop staff must schedule all other annual leave outside this two-week window. Logistics and Office staff have no blackout period and may request leave at any time during December subject to normal departmental scheduling.

## 4. Shift Schedule and Hours

### 4.1 Named Shifts and Times

BTC operates on a shift-based schedule with the following named shifts and hours (24-hour clock). The Morning Shift runs from 06:00 to 14:00 hours. The Afternoon Shift runs from 14:00 to 22:00 hours. The Night Shift runs from 22:00 to 06:00 hours. Office Hours are 09:00 to 17:00 hours.

### 4.2 Shift Assignments by Department

Workshop department staff work either the Morning Shift (06:00-14:00) or the Afternoon Shift (14:00-22:00). Workshop staff are never assigned to the Night Shift under any circumstances. Logistics department staff work the Morning Shift, Afternoon Shift, or Night Shift according to operational requirements and staffing needs. Office department staff work Office Hours (09:00-17:00) and are not scheduled for any other shift times. Sales department staff work Office Hours (09:00-17:00) to be available for customer contact during standard business hours. Shift assignments are determined by the department head and normally remain stable over time, though employees may be temporarily reassigned to different shifts for operational reasons with one week's notice.

### 4.3 Consecutive Night Shift Restriction

No employee may work two consecutive night shifts. If an employee is scheduled for a Night Shift, their next scheduled shift must be at least 24 hours later and must not be another Night Shift. This rule applies to all employees regardless of department or employment type.

### 4.4 Weekend Rules

Office and Sales department staff do not work on weekends (Saturday and Sunday). Workshop and Logistics staff may be required to work weekends as operational needs demand.

## 5. Overtime

### 5.1 Overtime Eligibility

Full-time and part-time employees may claim overtime compensation for hours worked in excess of their contracted weekly hours. Contractors may not claim overtime compensation under any circumstances.

### 5.2 Overtime Approval

Overtime must be approved in advance by the employee's Department Head. Overtime worked without prior approval is not guaranteed to be paid and may result in disciplinary action.

### 5.3 Overtime Hour Limits

All employees eligible for overtime (full-time and part-time) are limited to a maximum of 15 hours of overtime per calendar month. Any overtime hours beyond 15 in a single month are not reimbursed.

### 5.4 Overtime Compensation Rates

Overtime is compensated at a fixed hourly rate in credits (BTC's internal currency). Office staff receive 25 credits per overtime hour. Workshop staff receive 30 credits per overtime hour. Logistics staff receive 28 credits per overtime hour. Sales staff receive 22 credits per overtime hour.

## 6. Expenses and Reimbursement

### 6.1 Expense Categories and Limits

Employees who incur work-related expenses may submit them for reimbursement through the Finance department. A single expense item may not exceed 200 credits. This means that if a work-related purchase costs 201 credits or more, it is not eligible for reimbursement. The total reimbursement for any single business trip may not exceed 500 credits, regardless of the number of individual receipts or items included in the trip. A business trip is defined as a period of travel and activity away from the main office for work purposes lasting up to 5 consecutive calendar days. Trips lasting longer than 5 days require special approval from the Finance department and are not governed by the 500-credit limit.

### 6.2 Receipt and Documentation Requirements

Receipts are required for any expense item costing 50 credits or more. For expense items under 50 credits, no receipt is required but the employee must provide a brief written description of the item and its business purpose.

### 6.3 Approval Authority

Department Heads approve all expense reimbursements up to 200 credits per item. The Finance department approves all expense reimbursements exceeding 200 credits per item. For trip totals exceeding 500 credits, the Finance department must approve the reimbursement.

### 6.4 Non-Reimbursable Items

The following items are never reimbursed under any circumstances: personal meals and snacks, entertainment and social events, alcoholic beverages, non-work-related travel, personal hygiene products, and gifts.

## 7. Safety Training

### 7.1 Mandatory Safety Course

Workshop department staff and Logistics department staff are required to complete a mandatory safety course as a condition of employment in those departments. Office and Sales staff are not required to complete this course because their roles do not involve machinery operation. Contractors in the Workshop or Logistics departments are also required to complete the safety course before they may begin work, unless they provide valid certification from an external approved training provider recognized by BTC's Safety Coordinator. The safety course covers equipment operation, emergency procedures, personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements, and incident reporting.

context:
## Formation

Jupiter’s large Galilean moons – Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto – likely formed out of leftover material after Jupiter condensed from the initial cloud of gas and dust surrounding the sun, early in the history of the solar system. Those four moons are likely about the same age as the rest of the solar system – about 4.5 billion years old.

In fact, the Galilean moons are sometimes called a “mini solar system” since they formed from the leftovers of Jupiter similar to how Earth and other planets formed from gas and dust left over from the formation of the Sun. The similarities don’t end there. Each planet in the inner solar system is less dense than its inner neighbor – Mars is less dense than Earth, which is less dense than Venus, which is less dense than Mercury. The Galilean moons follow the same principle, being less dense the farther they are from Jupiter. The reduced density at greater distances is likely due to temperature: denser, rocky, and metal material condenses out first, close to Jupiter or the Sun, while lighter-weight icy material only condenses out at larger distances where it is colder.

Distance from Jupiter also determines how much tidal heating the Galilean satellites experience – Io, closest to Jupiter, is heated so much that it is the most volcanically-active body in the solar system. Ancient volcanic activity likely long ago evaporated any water it had when it formed. Europa has a layer of ice and water on top of a rocky and metal interior, while Ganymede and Callisto actually have higher proportions of water ice and lower densities.

## Structure

Like our planet, Europa is thought to have an iron core, a rocky mantle, and an ocean of salty water. Unlike Earth, however, Europa’s ocean lies below a shell of ice probably 10 to 15 miles (15 to 25 kilometers) thick, and has an estimated depth of 40 to 100 miles (60 to 150 kilometers). While evidence for an internal ocean is strong, its presence awaits confirmation by a future mission.

## Surface

Europa’s water-ice surface is crisscrossed by dark, reddish-brown cracks. Based on the small number of observable craters, the surface of this moon appears to be no more than 40 to 90 million years old, which is youthful in geologic terms (the surface of Callisto, another of Jupiter’s moons, is estimated to be a few billion years old). All along Europa's many fractures, and in splotchy patterns across its surface, is a reddish-brown material whose composition is not known for certain, but likely contains salts and sulfur compounds that have been mixed with the water ice and modified by radiation. This surface composition may hold clues to the moon's potential as a habitable world.

NASA's Galileo spacecraft explored the Jupiter system from 1995 to 2003 and made numerous flybys of Europa. Galileo revealed strange pits and domes that suggest Europa’s ice layer could be slowly churning, or convecting (cooler, denser ice sinks, while warmer less-dense ice rises) due to heat from below. Long, linear fractures are often only about a half mile to a mile wide (1-2 kilometers wide) but can extend for thousands of kilometers across Europa’s surface. Some of these fractures have built up into ridges hundreds of meters tall, while others appear to have pulled apart into wide bands of multiple parallel fractures.

Galileo also found regions called "chaos terrain," where broken, blocky landscapes were covered in mysterious reddish material. In 2011, scientists studying Galileo data proposed that chaos terrains could be places where the surface collapsed above lens-shaped lakes embedded within the ice.

## Atmosphere

Europa has only a tenuous atmosphere of oxygen, but in 2013, NASA announced that researchers using the Hubble Space Telescope found evidence that Europa might be actively venting water into space. This would mean the moon is geologically active in the present day.

In November 2019, an international research team led by NASA announced it had directly detected water vapor for the first time above Europa’s surface. If the plumes do exist, and if their source is linked to Europa’s ocean, then a spacecraft could travel through the plume to sample and analyze it from orbit, and it would essentially be analyzing the moon’s ocean. NASA’s Cassini spacecraft performed this feat at Saturn’s moon Enceladus, which is known to have an ocean spraying into space.

context:
Even if Europa isn’t ejecting samples into space, a 2018 study concluded that samples of Europa’s ocean could get frozen into the base of the moon’s ice shell, where the ice makes contact with the ocean. As the ice shell distorts and flexes from tidal forces, warmer and less-dense ice would rise, carrying the ocean samples to the surface where a spacecraft could analyze it remotely, using infrared and ultraviolet instruments, among others. Scientists could then study the material’s composition to determine whether Europa’s ocean might be hospitable for some form of life.

## Namesake

Europa is named for a woman who, in Greek mythology, was abducted by the god Zeus – Jupiter in Roman mythology.

## Potential for Life

Life as we know it seems to have three main requirements: liquid water, certain chemical elements, and an energy source. Also, life takes time to develop. Europa’s ocean may have existed for the entirety of our solar system’s history, approximately 4 billion years so sufficient time has passed for life to develop.

Astrobiologists – scientists who study the origin, evolution, and future of life in the universe – believe Europa has abundant water and the right chemical elements – the building blocks of life – including carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur.

The third ingredient for life is energy. All lifeforms need energy to survive. On Earth, most of that energy comes from the Sun. For example, plants grow and thrive through photosynthesis, a process that converts sunlight into energy. The energy is transferred to humans, animals, and other organisms when the plants are eaten.

But the type of life that might inhabit Europa likely would be powered purely by chemical reactions instead of by photosynthesis, because any life at Europa would exist beneath the ice, where there is no sunlight.

Europa's surface is blasted by radiation from Jupiter. That's a bad thing for life on the surface – it couldn't survive. But the radiation may create fuel for life in an ocean below the surface.

If we eventually find some form of life at Europa it may look like microbes, or maybe something more complex. If it can be demonstrated that life formed independently in two places around the same star, it would then be reasonable to suggest that life springs up in the universe fairly easily once the necessary ingredients are present, and that life might be found throughout our galaxy and the universe.

## Size and Distance

With an equatorial diameter of 1,940 miles (3,100 kilometers), Europa is about 90% the size of Earth’s Moon. So if we replaced our Moon with Europa, it would appear roughly the same size in the sky as our Moon does, but brighter – much, much brighter. Europa’s surface is made of water ice and so it reflects 5.5 times the sunlight than our Moon does.

Europa orbits Jupiter at about 417,000 miles (671,000 kilometers) from the planet, which itself orbits the Sun at a distance of roughly 500 million miles (780 million kilometers), or 5.2 astronomical units (AU). One AU is the distance from Earth to the Sun. Light from the Sun takes about 45 minutes to reach Europa. Because of the distance, sunlight is about 25 times fainter at Jupiter and Europa than at Earth.

## Orbit and Rotation

Europa orbits Jupiter every 3.5 days and is locked by gravity to Jupiter, so the same hemisphere of the moon always faces the planet. Jupiter takes about 4,333 Earth days (or about 12 Earth years) to orbit the Sun (a Jovian year). Jupiter’s equator (and the orbital plane of its moons) is tilted with respect to Jupiter’s orbital path around the Sun by only 3 degrees (Earth is tilted 23.5 degrees). This means Jupiter spins nearly upright so that the planet, as well as Europa and Jupiter’s other moons, do not have seasons like Earth.

Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are in what is called a resonance – every time Ganymede orbits Jupiter once, Europa orbits twice, and Io orbits four times. Over time, the orbits of most large satellites or planets tend to become circular, but in the case of these three satellites, the resonance produces a forced eccentricity since the satellites line up with each other at the same points in their orbits over and over, giving each other a small gravitational tug that keeps their orbits from becoming circular.

Because Europa's orbit is elliptical (slightly stretched out from circular), its distance from Jupiter varies, and the moon’s near side feels Jupiter’s gravity more strongly than its far side. The magnitude of this difference changes as Europa orbits, creating tides that stretch and relax the moon’s surface.

Flexing from the tides likely creates the moon’s surface fractures. If Europa's ocean exists, the tidal heating could also lead to volcanic or hydrothermal activity on the seafloor, supplying nutrients that could make the ocean suitable for living things.

## Namesake

Europa is named for a woman who, in Greek mythology, was abducted by the god Zeus – Jupiter in Roman mythology.

## Potential for Life

Life as we know it seems to have three main requirements: liquid water, certain chemical elements, and an energy source. Also, life takes time to develop. Europa’s ocean may have existed for the entirety of our solar system’s history, approximately 4 billion years so sufficient time has passed for life to develop.

Astrobiologists – scientists who study the origin, evolution, and future of life in the universe – believe Europa has abundant water and the right chemical elements – the building blocks of life – including carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur.

The third ingredient for life is energy. All lifeforms need energy to survive. On Earth, most of that energy comes from the Sun. For example, plants grow and thrive through photosynthesis, a process that converts sunlight into energy. The energy is transferred to humans, animals, and other organisms when the plants are eaten.

But the type of life that might inhabit Europa likely would be powered purely by chemical reactions instead of by photosynthesis, because any life at Europa would exist beneath the ice, where there is no sunlight.

Europa's surface is blasted by radiation from Jupiter. That's a bad thing for life on the surface – it couldn't survive. But the radiation may create fuel for life in an ocean below the surface.

If we eventually find some form of life at Europa it may look like microbes, or maybe something more complex. If it can be demonstrated that life formed independently in two places around the same star, it would then be reasonable to suggest that life springs up in the universe fairly easily once the necessary ingredients are present, and that life might be found throughout our galaxy and the universe.

## Size and Distance

With an equatorial diameter of 1,940 miles (3,100 kilometers), Europa is about 90% the size of Earth’s Moon. So if we replaced our Moon with Europa, it would appear roughly the same size in the sky as our Moon does, but brighter – much, much brighter. Europa’s surface is made of water ice and so it reflects 5.5 times the sunlight than our Moon does.

Europa orbits Jupiter at about 417,000 miles (671,000 kilometers) from the planet, which itself orbits the Sun at a distance of roughly 500 million miles (780 million kilometers), or 5.2 astronomical units (AU). One AU is the distance from Earth to the Sun. Light from the Sun takes about 45 minutes to reach Europa. Because of the distance, sunlight is about 25 times fainter at Jupiter and Europa than at Earth.

## Orbit and Rotation

Europa orbits Jupiter every 3.5 days and is locked by gravity to Jupiter, so the same hemisphere of the moon always faces the planet. Jupiter takes about 4,333 Earth days (or about 12 Earth years) to orbit the Sun (a Jovian year). Jupiter’s equator (and the orbital plane of its moons) is tilted with respect to Jupiter’s orbital path around the Sun by only 3 degrees (Earth is tilted 23.5 degrees). This means Jupiter spins nearly upright so that the planet, as well as Europa and Jupiter’s other moons, do not have seasons like Earth.

Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are in what is called a resonance – every time Ganymede orbits Jupiter once, Europa orbits twice, and Io orbits four times. Over time, the orbits of most large satellites or planets tend to become circular, but in the case of these three satellites, the resonance produces a forced eccentricity since the satellites line up with each other at the same points in their orbits over and over, giving each other a small gravitational tug that keeps their orbits from becoming circular.

Because Europa's orbit is elliptical (slightly stretched out from circular), its distance from Jupiter varies, and the moon’s near side feels Jupiter’s gravity more strongly than its far side. The magnitude of this difference changes as Europa orbits, creating tides that stretch and relax the moon’s surface.

Flexing from the tides likely creates the moon’s surface fractures. If Europa's ocean exists, the tidal heating could also lead to volcanic or hydrothermal activity on the seafloor, supplying nutrients that could make the ocean suitable for living things.

## Formation

Jupiter’s large Galilean moons – Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto – likely formed out of leftover material after Jupiter condensed from the initial cloud of gas and dust surrounding the sun, early in the history of the solar system. Those four moons are likely about the same age as the rest of the solar system – about 4.5 billion years old.

In fact, the Galilean moons are sometimes called a “mini solar system” since they formed from the leftovers of Jupiter similar to how Earth and other planets formed from gas and dust left over from the formation of the Sun. The similarities don’t end there. Each planet in the inner solar system is less dense than its inner neighbor – Mars is less dense than Earth, which is less dense than Venus, which is less dense than Mercury. The Galilean moons follow the same principle, being less dense the farther they are from Jupiter. The reduced density at greater distances is likely due to temperature: denser, rocky, and metal material condenses out first, close to Jupiter or the Sun, while lighter-weight icy material only condenses out at larger distances where it is colder.

Distance from Jupiter also determines how much tidal heating the Galilean satellites experience – Io, closest to Jupiter, is heated so much that it is the most volcanically-active body in the solar system. Ancient volcanic activity likely long ago evaporated any water it had when it formed. Europa has a layer of ice and water on top of a rocky and metal interior, while Ganymede and Callisto actually have higher proportions of water ice and lower densities.

## Structure

Like our planet, Europa is thought to have an iron core, a rocky mantle, and an ocean of salty water. Unlike Earth, however, Europa’s ocean lies below a shell of ice probably 10 to 15 miles (15 to 25 kilometers) thick, and has an estimated depth of 40 to 100 miles (60 to 150 kilometers). While evidence for an internal ocean is strong, its presence awaits confirmation by a future mission.

## Surface

Europa’s water-ice surface is crisscrossed by dark, reddish-brown cracks. Based on the small number of observable craters, the surface of this moon appears to be no more than 40 to 90 million years old, which is youthful in geologic terms (the surface of Callisto, another of Jupiter’s moons, is estimated to be a few billion years old). All along Europa's many fractures, and in splotchy patterns across its surface, is a reddish-brown material whose composition is not known for certain, but likely contains salts and sulfur compounds that have been mixed with the water ice and modified by radiation. This surface composition may hold clues to the moon's potential as a habitable world.

NASA's Galileo spacecraft explored the Jupiter system from 1995 to 2003 and made numerous flybys of Europa. Galileo revealed strange pits and domes that suggest Europa’s ice layer could be slowly churning, or convecting (cooler, denser ice sinks, while warmer less-dense ice rises) due to heat from below. Long, linear fractures are often only about a half mile to a mile wide (1-2 kilometers wide) but can extend for thousands of kilometers across Europa’s surface. Some of these fractures have built up into ridges hundreds of meters tall, while others appear to have pulled apart into wide bands of multiple parallel fractures.

Galileo also found regions called "chaos terrain," where broken, blocky landscapes were covered in mysterious reddish material. In 2011, scientists studying Galileo data proposed that chaos terrains could be places where the surface collapsed above lens-shaped lakes embedded within the ice.

## Atmosphere

Europa has only a tenuous atmosphere of oxygen, but in 2013, NASA announced that researchers using the Hubble Space Telescope found evidence that Europa might be actively venting water into space. This would mean the moon is geologically active in the present day.

In November 2019, an international research team led by NASA announced it had directly detected water vapor for the first time above Europa’s surface. If the plumes do exist, and if their source is linked to Europa’s ocean, then a spacecraft could travel through the plume to sample and analyze it from orbit, and it would essentially be analyzing the moon’s ocean. NASA’s Cassini spacecraft performed this feat at Saturn’s moon Enceladus, which is known to have an ocean spraying into space.

# Brindlewood Tooling Cooperative - Staff Handbook (excerpt, revision 3, effective 2026-01-01)

## 1. Definitions and Framework

### 1.1 Employment Categories

This handbook applies to all staff of Brindlewood Tooling Cooperative (BTC). Employment is categorized into three distinct types.

A full-time employee is any person employed by BTC on a contract for 35 or more hours per week. Full-time employees are entitled to all benefits described in this handbook.

A part-time employee is any person employed by BTC on a contract for fewer than 35 hours per week. Part-time employees receive benefits on a pro-rata basis unless otherwise specified in this excerpt.

A contractor is a self-employed person or a person employed by an external agency who provides services to BTC but is not directly employed by BTC. Contractors receive only those benefits explicitly listed as available to contractors in this handbook.

### 1.2 Tenure and Reference Date

Tenure is calculated in complete calendar months from an employee's start date. A start date is the first calendar day an employee works for BTC. The reference date for all tenure calculations and eligibility determinations in this handbook is 2026-03-01. All dates and tenure periods are evaluated as of this reference date. For example, an employee who started on 2025-03-15 would have 11 complete months of tenure as of 2026-03-01. An employee who started on 2024-03-01 would have exactly 24 complete months of tenure as of 2026-03-01. Tenure is never rounded and fractional months do not count toward tenure bands.

## 2. Remote Work Eligibility

### 2.1 Full-Time Employees

Full-time employees with at least 6 months of tenure may work remotely. The maximum number of remote work days per week is 3 days. Remote work must be arranged with the employee's immediate supervisor at least one week in advance.

### 2.2 Part-Time Employees

Part-time employees may work remotely up to 2 days per week, provided their employment contract permits remote work. No tenure requirement applies to part-time employees for remote work eligibility.

### 2.3 Workshop Department Exception

Exception: Workshop department staff may never work remotely under any circumstances. This applies to all employment categories—full-time, part-time, and contractors—in the Workshop department.

### 2.4 Logistics Department Remote Work

Logistics department staff may work remotely up to 2 days per week only if two conditions are met: they must be full-time or part-time employees (not contractors), AND they must have at least 3 months of tenure AND they must receive approval from their department head. Department heads may grant an exception to the 3-month tenure requirement for Logistics staff, provided the exception is documented in writing.

### 2.5 Office and Sales Departments

Office and Sales department staff who meet the tenure requirement (at least 6 months for full-time) may work remotely up to 4 days per week.

## 3. Annual Leave Entitlement

### 3.1 Full-Time Employee Leave by Tenure

Full-time employees receive annual leave (paid days off) according to their tenure as calculated on 2026-03-01. Employees with fewer than 2 complete years of tenure receive 20 days of leave per year. Employees with 2 to 5 complete years of tenure (inclusive) receive 23 days of leave per year. Employees with more than 5 complete years of tenure receive 26 days of leave per year.

### 3.2 Part-Time Employee Leave

Part-time employees receive 12 days of leave per year, regardless of tenure. This is a fixed entitlement and does not vary with length of service.

### 3.3 Contractor Leave

Contractors receive no annual leave entitlement. Contractors are not entitled to paid time off.

### 3.4 Leave Carry-Over

Unused leave may be carried over to the next calendar year up to a maximum of 5 days. Any leave in excess of 5 days at the end of a year is forfeited and cannot be carried forward or compensated.

### 3.5 Leave Blackout Period

Workshop staff may not take leave during the blackout period from 2026-12-01 to 2026-12-14 (the first two weeks of December), except in cases of emergency leave. Emergency leave in the blackout period must be approved by the Operations Manager in writing and is limited to genuine emergencies such as serious illness or family bereavement. Planned leave during the blackout period is not permitted for Workshop staff. This blackout period applies every December, following the same calendar dates each year. Workshop staff must schedule all other annual leave outside this two-week window. Logistics and Office staff have no blackout period and may request leave at any time during December subject to normal departmental scheduling.

In fact, the Galilean moons are sometimes called a “mini solar system” since they formed from the leftovers of Jupiter similar to how Earth and other planets formed from gas and dust left over from the formation of the Sun. The similarities don’t end there. Distance from Jupiter also determines how much tidal heating the Galilean satellites experience – Io, closest to Jupiter, is heated so much that it is the most volcanically-active body in the solar system. Ancient volcanic activity likely long ago evaporated any water it had when it formed. Europa has a layer of ice and water on top of a rocky and metal interior, while Ganymede and Callisto actually have higher proportions of water ice and lower densities.

## Structure

Like our planet, Europa is thought to have an iron core, a rocky mantle, and an ocean of salty water. Unlike Earth, however, Europa’s ocean lies below a shell of ice probably 10 to 15 miles (15 to 25 kilometers) thick, and has an estimated depth of 40 to 100 miles (60 to 150 kilometers). While evidence for an internal ocean is strong, its presence awaits confirmation by a future mission.

## Surface

Europa’s water-ice surface is crisscrossed by dark, reddish-brown cracks. Based on the small number of observable craters, the surface of this moon appears to be no more than 40 to 90 million years old, which is youthful in geologic terms (the surface of Callisto, another of Jupiter’s moons, is estimated to be a few billion years old). All along Europa's many fractures, and in splotchy patterns across its surface, is a reddish-brown material whose composition is not known for certain, but likely contains salts and sulfur compounds that have been mixed with the water ice and modified by radiation. This surface composition may hold clues to the moon's potential as a habitable world.

### 4.1 Named Shifts and Times

BTC operates on a shift-based schedule with the following named shifts and hours (24-hour clock). The Morning Shift runs from 06:00 to 14:00 hours. The Afternoon Shift runs from 14:00 to 22:00 hours. The Night Shift runs from 22:00 to 06:00 hours. Office Hours are 09:00 to 17:00 hours.

### 4.2 Shift Assignments by Department

Workshop department staff work either the Morning Shift (06:00-14:00) or the Afternoon Shift (14:00-22:00). Workshop staff are never assigned to the Night Shift under any circumstances. Logistics department staff work the Morning Shift, Afternoon Shift, or Night Shift according to operational requirements and staffing needs. Office department staff work Office Hours (09:00-17:00) and are not scheduled for any other shift times. Sales department staff work Office Hours (09:00-17:00) to be available for customer contact during standard business hours. Shift assignments are determined by the department head and normally remain stable over time, though employees may be temporarily reassigned to different shifts for operational reasons with one week's notice.

### 4.3 Consecutive Night Shift Restriction

No employee may work two consecutive night shifts. If an employee is scheduled for a Night Shift, their next scheduled shift must be at least 24 hours later and must not be another Night Shift. This rule applies to all employees regardless of department or employment type.

### 4.4 Weekend Rules

Office and Sales department staff do not work on weekends (Saturday and Sunday). Workshop and Logistics staff may be required to work weekends as operational needs demand.

## 5. Overtime

### 5.1 Overtime Eligibility

Full-time and part-time employees may claim overtime compensation for hours worked in excess of their contracted weekly hours. Contractors may not claim overtime compensation under any circumstances.

### 5.2 Overtime Approval

Overtime must be approved in advance by the employee's Department Head. Overtime worked without prior approval is not guaranteed to be paid and may result in disciplinary action.

### 5.3 Overtime Hour Limits

All employees eligible for overtime (full-time and part-time) are limited to a maximum of 15 hours of overtime per calendar month. Any overtime hours beyond 15 in a single month are not reimbursed.

### 5.4 Overtime Compensation Rates

Overtime is compensated at a fixed hourly rate in credits (BTC's internal currency). Office staff receive 25 credits per overtime hour. Workshop staff receive 30 credits per overtime hour. Logistics staff receive 28 credits per overtime hour. Sales staff receive 22 credits per overtime hour.

## 6. Expenses and Reimbursement

### 6.1 Expense Categories and Limits

Employees who incur work-related expenses may submit them for reimbursement through the Finance department. A single expense item may not exceed 200 credits. This means that if a work-related purchase costs 201 credits or more, it is not eligible for reimbursement. The total reimbursement for any single business trip may not exceed 500 credits, regardless of the number of individual receipts or items included in the trip. A business trip is defined as a period of travel and activity away from the main office for work purposes lasting up to 5 consecutive calendar days. Trips lasting longer than 5 days require special approval from the Finance department and are not governed by the 500-credit limit.

### 6.2 Receipt and Documentation Requirements

Receipts are required for any expense item costing 50 credits or more. For expense items under 50 credits, no receipt is required but the employee must provide a brief written description of the item and its business purpose.

### 6.3 Approval Authority

Department Heads approve all expense reimbursements up to 200 credits per item. The Finance department approves all expense reimbursements exceeding 200 credits per item. For trip totals exceeding 500 credits, the Finance department must approve the reimbursement.

### 6.4 Non-Reimbursable Items

The following items are never reimbursed under any circumstances: personal meals and snacks, entertainment and social events, alcoholic beverages, non-work-related travel, personal hygiene products, and gifts.

## 7. Safety Training

### 7.1 Mandatory Safety Course

Workshop department staff and Logistics department staff are required to complete a mandatory safety course as a condition of employment in those departments. Office and Sales staff are not required to complete this course because their roles do not involve machinery operation. Contractors in the Workshop or Logistics departments are also required to complete the safety course before they may begin work, unless they provide valid certification from an external approved training provider recognized by BTC's Safety Coordinator. The safety course covers equipment operation, emergency procedures, personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements, and incident reporting.

# Brindlewood Tooling Cooperative - Staff Handbook (excerpt, revision 3, effective 2026-01-01)

## 1. Definitions and Framework

### 1.1 Employment Categories

This handbook applies to all staff of Brindlewood Tooling Cooperative (BTC). Employment is categorized into three distinct types.

A full-time employee is any person employed by BTC on a contract for 35 or more hours per week. Full-time employees are entitled to all benefits described in this handbook.

A part-time employee is any person employed by BTC on a contract for fewer than 35 hours per week. Part-time employees receive benefits on a pro-rata basis unless otherwise specified in this excerpt.

A contractor is a self-employed person or a person employed by an external agency who provides services to BTC but is not directly employed by BTC. Contractors receive only those benefits explicitly listed as available to contractors in this handbook.

### 1.2 Tenure and Reference Date

Tenure is calculated in complete calendar months from an employee's start date. A start date is the first calendar day an employee works for BTC. The reference date for all tenure calculations and eligibility determinations in this handbook is 2026-03-01. All dates and tenure periods are evaluated as of this reference date. For example, an employee who started on 2025-03-15 would have 11 complete months of tenure as of 2026-03-01. An employee who started on 2024-03-01 would have exactly 24 complete months of tenure as of 2026-03-01. Tenure is never rounded and fractional months do not count toward tenure bands.

## 2. Remote Work Eligibility

### 2.1 Full-Time Employees

Full-time employees with at least 6 months of tenure may work remotely. The maximum number of remote work days per week is 3 days. Remote work must be arranged with the employee's immediate supervisor at least one week in advance.

### 2.2 Part-Time Employees

Part-time employees may work remotely up to 2 days per week, provided their employment contract permits remote work. No tenure requirement applies to part-time employees for remote work eligibility.

### 2.3 Workshop Department Exception

Exception: Workshop department staff may never work remotely under any circumstances. This applies to all employment categories—full-time, part-time, and contractors—in the Workshop department.

### 2.4 Logistics Department Remote Work

Logistics department staff may work remotely up to 2 days per week only if two conditions are met: they must be full-time or part-time employees (not contractors), AND they must have at least 3 months of tenure AND they must receive approval from their department head. Department heads may grant an exception to the 3-month tenure requirement for Logistics staff, provided the exception is documented in writing.

### 2.5 Office and Sales Departments

Office and Sales department staff who meet the tenure requirement (at least 6 months for full-time) may work remotely up to 4 days per week.

## 3. Annual Leave Entitlement

### 3.1 Full-Time Employee Leave by Tenure

Full-time employees receive annual leave (paid days off) according to their tenure as calculated on 2026-03-01. Employees with fewer than 2 complete years of tenure receive 20 days of leave per year. Employees with 2 to 5 complete years of tenure (inclusive) receive 23 days of leave per year. Employees with more than 5 complete years of tenure receive 26 days of leave per year.

### 3.2 Part-Time Employee Leave

Part-time employees receive 12 days of leave per year, regardless of tenure. This is a fixed entitlement and does not vary with length of service.

### 3.3 Contractor Leave

Contractors receive no annual leave entitlement. Contractors are not entitled to paid time off.

### 3.4 Leave Carry-Over

Unused leave may be carried over to the next calendar year up to a maximum of 5 days. Any leave in excess of 5 days at the end of a year is forfeited and cannot be carried forward or compensated.

### 3.5 Leave Blackout Period

Workshop staff may not take leave during the blackout period from 2026-12-01 to 2026-12-14 (the first two weeks of December), except in cases of emergency leave. Emergency leave in the blackout period must be approved by the Operations Manager in writing and is limited to genuine emergencies such as serious illness or family bereavement. Planned leave during the blackout period is not permitted for Workshop staff. This blackout period applies every December, following the same calendar dates each year. Workshop staff must schedule all other annual leave outside this two-week window. Logistics and Office staff have no blackout period and may request leave at any time during December subject to normal departmental scheduling.

context:
Even if Europa isn’t ejecting samples into space, a 2018 study concluded that samples of Europa’s ocean could get frozen into the base of the moon’s ice shell, where the ice makes contact with the ocean. As the ice shell distorts and flexes from tidal forces, warmer and less-dense ice would rise, carrying the ocean samples to the surface where a spacecraft could analyze it remotely, using infrared and ultraviolet instruments, among others. Scientists could then study the material’s composition to determine whether Europa’s ocean might be hospitable for some form of life.

## Namesake

Europa is named for a woman who, in Greek mythology, was abducted by the god Zeus – Jupiter in Roman mythology.

## Potential for Life

Life as we know it seems to have three main requirements: liquid water, certain chemical elements, and an energy source. Also, life takes time to develop. Europa’s ocean may have existed for the entirety of our solar system’s history, approximately 4 billion years so sufficient time has passed for life to develop.

Astrobiologists – scientists who study the origin, evolution, and future of life in the universe – believe Europa has abundant water and the right chemical elements – the building blocks of life – including carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur.

The third ingredient for life is energy. All lifeforms need energy to survive. On Earth, most of that energy comes from the Sun. For example, plants grow and thrive through photosynthesis, a process that converts sunlight into energy. The energy is transferred to humans, animals, and other organisms when the plants are eaten.

But the type of life that might inhabit Europa likely would be powered purely by chemical reactions instead of by photosynthesis, because any life at Europa would exist beneath the ice, where there is no sunlight.

Europa's surface is blasted by radiation from Jupiter. That's a bad thing for life on the surface – it couldn't survive. But the radiation may create fuel for life in an ocean below the surface.

If we eventually find some form of life at Europa it may look like microbes, or maybe something more complex. If it can be demonstrated that life formed independently in two places around the same star, it would then be reasonable to suggest that life springs up in the universe fairly easily once the necessary ingredients are present, and that life might be found throughout our galaxy and the universe.

## Size and Distance

With an equatorial diameter of 1,940 miles (3,100 kilometers), Europa is about 90% the size of Earth’s Moon. So if we replaced our Moon with Europa, it would appear roughly the same size in the sky as our Moon does, but brighter – much, much brighter. Europa’s surface is made of water ice and so it reflects 5.5 times the sunlight than our Moon does.

Europa orbits Jupiter at about 417,000 miles (671,000 kilometers) from the planet, which itself orbits the Sun at a distance of roughly 500 million miles (780 million kilometers), or 5.2 astronomical units (AU). One AU is the distance from Earth to the Sun. Light from the Sun takes about 45 minutes to reach Europa. Because of the distance, sunlight is about 25 times fainter at Jupiter and Europa than at Earth.

## Orbit and Rotation

Europa orbits Jupiter every 3.5 days and is locked by gravity to Jupiter, so the same hemisphere of the moon always faces the planet. Jupiter takes about 4,333 Earth days (or about 12 Earth years) to orbit the Sun (a Jovian year). Jupiter’s equator (and the orbital plane of its moons) is tilted with respect to Jupiter’s orbital path around the Sun by only 3 degrees (Earth is tilted 23.5 degrees). This means Jupiter spins nearly upright so that the planet, as well as Europa and Jupiter’s other moons, do not have seasons like Earth.

Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are in what is called a resonance – every time Ganymede orbits Jupiter once, Europa orbits twice, and Io orbits four times. Over time, the orbits of most large satellites or planets tend to become circular, but in the case of these three satellites, the resonance produces a forced eccentricity since the satellites line up with each other at the same points in their orbits over and over, giving each other a small gravitational tug that keeps their orbits from becoming circular.

Because Europa's orbit is elliptical (slightly stretched out from circular), its distance from Jupiter varies, and the moon’s near side feels Jupiter’s gravity more strongly than its far side. The magnitude of this difference changes as Europa orbits, creating tides that stretch and relax the moon’s surface.

Flexing from the tides likely creates the moon’s surface fractures. If Europa's ocean exists, the tidal heating could also lead to volcanic or hydrothermal activity on the seafloor, supplying nutrients that could make the ocean suitable for living things.
